title: Network Analysis of Hospital Financial Data: Stability, Group Differences, and Relevance to Closure
content: (Background) Hospital financial and operating measures are interdependent, but it is unknown whether this structure is stable over time, whether it differs across hospitals and communities, and whether a hospital's position within it carries information about survival. (Objective) To describe year-by-year networks of hospital characteristics, identify what predicts network structure and position, and test whether position forecasts closure. (Methods) Medicare cost reports for US short-term acute care and critical access hospitals (2011–2020; reports of 150–366 days) provided 13 characteristics. Correlation and partial correlation networks were estimated for each year and for groups defined by payment type, setting, ownership, size and county conditions. Two hospital-level measures of network position, Mahalanobis distance from the annual center and profile inconsistency, were related to hospital and community characteristics and to closure in the following year. (Results) Network density was stable across 2011–2019 (mean absolute correlation 0.132 to 0.141; no trend, p = 0.905). Networks were denser among for-profit (0.177) and government hospitals (0.184) than nonprofit hospitals (0.138) and among large than small hospitals (0.165 versus 0.125). Critical access, for-profit, government and larger hospitals, and hospitals in poorer counties and counties with larger Black populations, sat further from the network center. Hospitals that closed had more inconsistent profiles (0.706 versus 0.522), and adding network position raised cross-validated discrimination from 0.771 to 0.810 (difference +0.039; 95% CI, 0.019 to 0.058); profile inconsistency carried an odds ratio of 2.49 per standard deviation. (Conclusions) The structure of hospital finances is stable over time but differs by ownership, payment and community, and how a hospital's measures fit together forecasts closure beyond their levels.
